Formulation
- Predisposing factors: personal history of asthma; family history of asthma and eczema; atopic tendency (hay fever, possible eczema).
- Precipitating factors: recent exertion (running with friend) 2–3 days ago precipitated acute shortness of breath/wheeze.
- Perpetuating factors: time since last asthma review (~2 years); irregular or unclear preventer/inhaler regimen; infrequent peak flow monitoring.
- Protective factors: no prior severe exacerbations requiring admission, patient has access to rescue inhaler, clinician provided interim management steps and advised prompt GP review and A&E if worsening.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Suspected acute asthma exacerbation (wheeze, cough, shortness of breath)
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Reduce breathlessness and wheeze to baseline
  - Avoid emergency admission
  - Attend face-to-face clinical review within days
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Assess severity with clinical exam and peak flow
  - Optimize inhaler regimen and provide rescue/acute treatment if needed (oral steroids/antibiotics if indicated)
  - Establish an updated asthma action plan and follow-up
- Actions (Patient):
  - Continue using blue inhaler (salbutamol) as needed; maximum interim use advised up to every 2–4 hours (as instructed by clinician)
  - Increase brown preventer (Clenil) to four puffs twice daily while awaiting review (per clinician advice)
  - Monitor symptoms and seek immediate care (A&E) if breathing significantly worsens or does not improve
  - Book and attend face-to-face GP appointment in the next few days for assessment, peak flow, and possible further treatment
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Arrange face-to-face review within next few days for chest examination, peak flow measurement, and assessment of need for oral steroids and/or antibiotics
  - Review and clarify inhaler types, doses, and technique; provide or update asthma action plan
  - Provide urgent escalation (A&E) instructions if symptoms worsen prior to review

Secondary Problem: Atopic skin disease / hay fever (possible eczema)
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Control skin symptoms and hay fever
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Clarify diagnosis (eczema vs other skin conditions), review topical medications and usage
- Actions (Patient):
  - Continue topical medications as currently used (Cetraben, Bactroban, hydrocortisone) as previously instructed by other clinicians
  - Report skin symptom details at GP review
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Review dermatologic symptoms at face-to-face appointment and advise on appropriate topical regimen or referral if required

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered:
  - Nature of current respiratory symptoms and likely small exacerbation
  - Interim inhaler management: salbutamol PRN (up to every 2–4 hours temporarily); increase brown Clenil to four puffs twice daily while awaiting review
  - Need to attend face-to-face GP review in next few days for chest exam and peak flow; possible need for oral steroids/antibiotics depending on findings
  - When to go to A&E: breathing significantly worse despite interim measures
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening:
  - Increasing use of blue inhaler (needing every 2–4 hours or more)
  - Progressive worsening of breathlessness or wheeze
  - Reduced peak flow compared with usual (~380 L/min reported as typical)
- Coping Strategies:
  - Use prescribed inhalers as directed
  - Monitor symptoms and peak flow if available
  - Seek urgent medical attention (A&E) if symptoms worsen

Quality checks
● Missing but clinically expected elements: explicit diagnostic confirmation (spirometry/peak flow values at time of assessment), formal asthma action plan documented, explicit medication doses for current regimen, mental health history/assessment not recorded, suicide/self-harm risk assessment not recorded.  
● Internal conflicts from the transcript: uncertainty/conflict regarding which inhaler is the preventer (patient initially confused about colors/names); medication list and exact doses/routes for topical and inhaled drugs not clearly documented.  
● Transcript quality notes: Some audio/dialogue unclear at points (patient name not captured), medication names and doses clarified mid-consult; address transcribed in words rather than standardized format.
